answer.label: Not Virginia Woolf — an unsourced internet quotation
answer.sourceLine: The line is usually credited to Woolf’s 1919 novel Night and Day, but the Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ says it is “not in Night and Day, nor anywhere else in Woolf’s works.” The earliest online appearance the Society found is dated 15 November 2012. No one has identified who first wrote it.

source.excerpt: What if I told you I’m incapable of tolerating my own heart?
trail: The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ lists the line as a misattribution: “Source: None. This not in Night and Day, nor anywhere else in Woolf’s works.” It says the earliest online occurrence it found is dated 15 November 2012.
A Penguin Books UK article ↗ on Woolf quotations prints the line and credits it to Night and Day. The Society names this page as one place it found the line.
The full text of Night and Day is free at Project Gutenberg ↗. A keyword search of that text finds no “tolerating” and no sentence like this one.
Woolf’s Wikiquote page ↗ does not list the line. Its Misattributed section points readers to the Society’s misquotations page.
source.excerptNote: No fuller original passage exists. The Society says the line is not in Night and Day or anywhere else in Woolf’s writing. In a keyword search of the Project Gutenberg text of the novel, the word “tolerating” never appears.

author.name: Virginia Woolf
author.heading: About Virginia Woolf
author.bio: Virginia Woolf wrote Mrs Dalloway, To the Lighthouse and A Room of One’s Own, and is one of the most quoted modernist writers. Night and Day, the novel this line is usually credited to, was her second novel, first published in 1919. Woolf did not write this line: it is one of many internet “Woolf quotes” that the Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain has found in none of her works.

misattribution.heading: How a modern line became “Woolf”
misattribution.intro: The line is usually given with a specific-sounding source, “Night and Day,” and that has helped it pass as genuine. It has been repeated in places readers tend to trust: a publisher’s website and printed books.

items.why: Penguin's article on Woolf quotations ↗ ends with the line, credited “(Night and Day)”. The Virginia Woolf Society ↗ says two of the article’s twelve quotations are not genuine, and this is one of them.
According to the Virginia Woolf Society ↗, the line is the book’s epigraph, attributed to “Virginia Woolf, Night and Day” (Little, Brown Books for Young Readers, 2017).
The Virginia Woolf Society ↗ reports that this Welsh-language memoir (Y Lolfa, 2018) quotes the line in English as if it came from Night and Day.
Quotewise ↗ credits the line to Virginia Woolf and names no work or date on the page. The Society says the line “has spread across blogs like a rash.”

misattribution.truthLine: Woolf did not write this. The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ finds it in none of her works, and the earliest online appearance it found dates from 2012. Its true author is unknown.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The line has the confessional, inward tone many readers associate with Woolf, and it is usually given a precise-sounding citation, “Night and Day.” A named novel makes a quotation look checked, even when no one has looked. In this case, anyone who searches the novel’s text will not find the sentence.

Once a publisher's website and printed books repeated the line, later readers had what looked like solid sources to copy from. The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ keeps its misquotations page so that lines like this one can be traced and corrected.
